content: The document outlines a framework for tuberculosis (TB) management, prevention, and care during humanitarian emergencies. It emphasizes the prioritization of interventions for an initial minimum response during emergencies, followed by a comprehensive response as soon as feasible. Each chapter provides detailed references to support workforce development and program design. The introduction highlights the importance of ensuring safe transport for individuals with infectious TB and screening patients for pandemic illnesses. It also defines key terms such as antiretroviral treatment (ART), bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and tuberculosis (TB). The background section discusses the increased vulnerability of populations affected by humanitarian emergencies to infectious diseases like TB. Refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs) are particularly at risk due to poor living conditions, limited access to healthcare, and comorbidities such as HIV and diabetes. These factors weaken the immune system, increasing susceptibility to TB. The chapter also highlights the global displacement crisis, with millions of people requiring humanitarian assistance, and the disproportionate burden on developing countries hosting refugees and IDPs. TB prevention and care among refugees and displaced populations face significant challenges, including crowded living conditions, poor nutrition, and interrupted healthcare services. These factors facilitate TB transmission and hinder treatment continuity, leading to the spread of drug-resistant TB. Access to TB medicines is often compromised in emergency settings due to overwhelmed health infrastructure. The document emphasizes the integration of TB prevention and care into humanitarian responses, guided by global commitments such as the New York Declaration for Refugees and Migrants, the Global Compact on Refugees, and the WHO End TB Strategy. These frameworks aim to uphold the right to health for all, including refugees and displaced populations, and to achieve ambitious targets for ending the TB epidemic by 2030. The WHO End TB Strategy focuses on patient-centered care, early diagnosis, treatment of drug-resistant TB, and prevention through vaccination and systematic screening. It also calls for bold policies, strong community engagement, universal health coverage, and intensified research to develop new tools and strategies. The COVID-19 pandemic has severely impacted global TB control efforts, reversing years of progress. Disruptions in healthcare services have led to fewer TB diagnoses and treatments, with vulnerable populations, including refugees, disproportionately affected. The pandemic has highlighted the need for resilient health systems and the importance of ensuring access to essential TB services during crises. WHO, UNHCR, and CDC have been working collaboratively to address the needs of vulnerable populations during the COVID-19 pandemic, ensuring continuity of TB services and learning lessons to strengthen preparedness for future emergencies. These efforts aim to build stronger health systems and ensure no one is left behind, particularly among the most at-risk populations.
